claims.text: THE SIZES HAVE DRIFTED, AND THE DRIFT RUNS ONE WAY, across three opened documents. The 1990 interview notes give 'The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.' The April 2001 Briefing Document gives the smallest as 'about 24 feet in diameter at its widest part, right at the base', the next as '60 feet in diameter at the base', and 'the largest of these vehicles was about 120 to 130 feet in diameter'. The arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, read 18 September 2026, gives 'one with a 130-foot diameter, another with a 60-foot diameter, and a smaller one measuring 24 feet in diameter', with no disclaimer. Each retelling is more precise than the last about a figure the witness explicitly refused to stand behind.

claims.text: The account attributes the claimed lift effect to Thomas Townsend Brown. The 2001 testimony describes an experiment by 'Mark Stambough' that floated a plate capacitor at about a million volts 'in accordance with principles that had been described in a patent that was filed back in the late 1950s/early 1960s by a gentleman called Thomas Townsend Brown. Brown and another individual by the name of Dr. Biefield had done this, so this effect became known as the Biefield-Brown effect.' The direction of motion is given as toward the positively charged plate. The board's own record of both candidate patents is that NEITHER claims anti-gravity: US 3,187,206, filed 9 May 1958, opens 'This invention relates to an electrical device for producing thrust by the direct operation of electrical fields', and US 2,949,550, filed 3 July 1957, claims 'Thrust producing apparatus' operating by impressing high voltage between a body and an insulated electrode 'whereby to cause relative movement of an ionizable dielectric medium'. It is the ACCOUNT that reinterprets electrokinetic thrust as levitation.

claims.text: A CORRECTION THIS BOARD MAKES AGAINST ITS OWN SIDE OF THE ARGUMENT. The objection commonly made to Wolfe, that he dated the episode to 1965 when no Lunar Orbiter had flown, DOES NOT APPLY TO THIS DOCUMENT AND IS NOT ASSERTED HERE. The Briefing Document gives no year for the episode. It gives a service window of January 1964 plus four and a half years, which runs to about mid-1968 and therefore encloses the Lunar Orbiter photographic period of August 1966 to August 1967. Anyone wishing to make the chronology objection must first open the later Wolfe source in which he gave that date. This board did not open one.

edges.label: Attributes the claimed lift effect to a Brown patent of the late 1950s or early 1960s
edges.note: THE EDGE MUST NOT BE READ AS ANTI-GRAVITY. The board's own record is that NEITHER Brown patent claims anti-gravity: US 3,187,206, filed 9 May 1958, and US 2,949,550, filed 3 July 1957, both claim thrust by electrical fields in a dielectric medium. It is the ACCOUNT that reinterprets electrokinetic thrust as levitation. His testimony describes a plate capacitor floated at about a million volts 'in accordance with principles that had been described in a patent that was filed back in the late 1950s/early 1960s by a gentleman called Thomas Townsend Brown'.
